You are helping a researcher prepare for an upcoming academic conference on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). The conference is called "RLHF Summit 2026" and will take place on April 10, 2026 from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM at the San Francisco Convention Center.

First, search the academic paper databases for papers related to "reinforcement learning from human feedback". You should find at least 5 relevant papers. Exclude any papers that are not directly about RLHF or human feedback in the context of language model training (for example, papers about self-play in board games should be excluded).

For each of the relevant RLHF papers you find, retrieve the full manuscript source to examine their methodology sections in detail. Pay attention to the key techniques each paper introduces.

Next, create a PowerPoint presentation called RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx in your workspace. The presentation should include the following slides:

First, a title slide with the title "RLHF Summit 2026 Conference Preparation Report" and subtitle "Key Papers in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback".

First, an overview slide that introduces the field of RLHF and why it matters for language model alignment.

First, one slide for each of the relevant papers (at least 5 slides). Each paper slide should include the paper title, the authors, and a brief summary of the key contribution and methodology. Make sure to include papers about instruction following with human feedback, learning to summarize from human feedback, constitutional AI, direct preference optimization, and proximal policy optimization.

First, a summary slide that synthesizes the key themes across all papers.

After creating the presentation, create a calendar event for the RLHF Summit 2026 conference. The event should be on April 10, 2026 from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, with the location set to "San Francisco Convention Center" and a description that mentions this is a conference about reinforcement learning from human feedback.

Finally, send an email to your collaborators at collaborators@rlhf-lab.org with the subject "RLHF Summit 2026 Preparation Materials". The email body should briefly describe that you have prepared a conference report covering key RLHF papers and created a calendar event for the conference. Mention the date (April 10, 2026) and location in the email.

If you are working in a multi-agent setup, designate exactly one agent to create and write RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx, and have the other agents coordinate with it — do not have multiple agents write to the same file, as concurrent writers can overwrite each other.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, follow this exact orchestration plan. A wave must finish and return all stated handoffs before the next wave begins. Within a wave, dispatch exactly one sub-agent for each numbered sub-task and run those sub-agents concurrently.

Before Wave 1, the main agent must freeze exactly five required paper slots—InstructGPT, learning to summarize from human feedback, Constitutional AI, DPO, and PPO—and the conference, presentation, calendar, and email contract. It must assign one stable paper identity per slot and exclude unrelated human-feedback or self-play work. Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Because the conference event is fixed and independent of paper research, the main agent must search for the exact event before dispatch and, in the same orchestration response that launches Wave 1, create at most the one missing event for 2026-04-10 from 09:00 to 17:00 at `San Francisco Convention Center`; preserve the calendar tool's default timezone, use no attendees, and retain the event ID for later read-back. Do not retry creation after an ambiguous failure.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 sub-agents in parallel, one for each numbered sub-task:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Use one explore sub-agent to research instruction following with human feedback.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Use one explore sub-agent to research learning to summarize from human feedback.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Use one explore sub-agent to research Constitutional AI.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Use one explore sub-agent to research Direct Preference Optimization.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Use one explore sub-agent to research Proximal Policy Optimization.

Each Wave 1 sub-agent must search the granted academic sources read-only for only its assigned slot, validate title/abstract relevance, retrieve the full available manuscript/source, and return a compact source-backed record with authors, contribution, methodology, stable ID/title, source/section coverage, and missing-field status. Explore is read-only, so do not write files or create slides, calendar events, or email.

After Wave 1, the main agent must reconcile the five stable IDs and distinguish PPO's foundational algorithm role from direct language-model alignment evidence; it must freeze one literal canonical five-paper packet and reject invented claims. The deck and final email consume exactly this packet without re-researching or rephrasing factual fields.

2. Wave 2 — dispatch exactly 1 sub-agent for the following numbered sub-task:

   1. coder 0 (office-report-builder 0): Use one coder sub-agent to own `<workspace_root>/RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx` exclusively. To avoid a long sequence of slide-by-slide calls, use one `python_execute` with the installed `python-pptx` package to create the complete deck atomically from the canonical packet: required title and overview slides, exactly one substantive slide for each of the five frozen papers, and a final synthesis slide. Then use the presentation read tools once to verify slide count, titles, five-paper coverage, and source-backed authors/methods. Return path and validation; do not create calendar or email state.

After Wave 2, the main agent must verify the deck and read back the retained calendar event, requiring exactly one matching RLHF Summit 2026 event on 2026-04-10 from 09:00 to 17:00 at the specified location. It must then search sent mail and send at most one missing email to collaborators@rlhf-lab.org with the exact subject and verified report/event details. Perform final deck, event, and message checks before completion.

Goal: Produce a compact, source-backed record for this ONE paper. Do NOT research other papers.

Steps:
1. Use the granted read-only academic tools (mcp__arxiv-latex__* and mcp__scholarly__search-arxiv) to locate the paper. The expected stable arXiv ID is 2203.02155 — verify it by title/abstract.
2. Validate relevance: the paper must be about RLHF / human feedback in the context of language model training (instruction following). If 2203.02155 does not match, search "training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" and pick the correct InstructGPT paper.
3. Retrieve the full manuscript source (use mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_prompt for the flattened LaTeX, or get_paper_section for methodology sections; list_paper_sections to find them). Research PPO paper

You are the office-report builder. You own the file `<workspace_root>/RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx` EXCLUSIVELY — no other agent will write it. Do NOT create calendar events or send emails.

Workspace root (use exactly this path, do NOT use bare /workspace):
`/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-conference-prep/workspace`

Goal: Create the presentation `RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx` in that directory, then verify it with the pptx read tools.

STEP 1 — Build the deck atomically with one `mcp__local__python_execute` call using the installed `python-pptx` package. The deck must have exactly 8 slides:

Slide 1 (Title): title "RLHF Summit 2026 Conference Preparation Report", subtitle "Key Papers in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback".

Slide 2 (Overview): "Overview: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback" — introduce the field and why it matters for language model alignment. Content: RLHF aligns large language models with human preferences and intent by training a reward model on human judgments and optimizing the policy against it (typically with PPO); it is the core technique behind instruction-following assistants and helps improve helpfulness, truthfulness, and harmlessness of aligned models.

Slides 3–7 (one per paper — use EXACTLY this frozen, source-backed packet; do not rephrase factual fields, do not invent facts):

--- Paper 1: InstructGPT ---
Title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT)
Authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, Chong Zhang, Sandhini Agarwal, Katarina Slama, Alex Ray, John Schulman, et al. (NeurIPS 2022; arXiv 2203.02155)
Contribution: Shows that scaling model size alone does not make language models better at following user intent; aligning GPT-3 with human feedback produces InstructGPT, which human evaluators prefer over the much larger GPT-3 (a 1.3B InstructGPT preferred over 175B GPT-3), with improved truthfulness and reduced toxicity.
Methodology: Three-stage pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on labeler demonstrations of desired behavior; (2) reward model trained on human rankings of model outputs; (3) RLHF fine-tuning of the policy against the reward model using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a KL penalty to stay near the SFT model. Trained on labeler-written and API prompts; evaluated by human raters plus TruthfulQA/RealToxicityPrompts benchmarks.

--- Paper 2: Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback ---
Title: Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback
Authors: Nisan Stiennon, Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Daniel Ziegler, Ryan Lowe, Chelsea Voss, Alec Radford, Dario Amodei, Paul Christiano (NeurIPS 2020; arXiv 2009.01325)
Contribution: Early landmark demonstration of RLHF: optimizes summarization models directly for human preferences. Human evaluators prefer summaries from the RL-fine-tuned policy over supervised-learning-only baselines (~61% of the time).
Methodology: A reward model is trained on human comparisons of summaries; it scores a (post, summary) pair with a scalar reward. A summarization policy is then fine-tuned with PPO using this reward model, with KL regularization to keep the policy near the supervised baseline. Task/data: abstractive summarization of Reddit posts (TL;DR dataset); evaluation by human raters.

--- Paper 3: Constitutional AI ---
Title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
Authors: Yuntao Bai, Saurav Kadavath, Sandipan Kundu, Amanda Askell, Jackson Kernion, Andy Jones, Anna Chen, Anna Goldie, Azalia Mirhoseini, Cameron McKinnon, et al. (arXiv 2022; arXiv 2212.08073)
Contribution: Introduces Constitutional AI (CAI): training a harmless assistant using a set of principles (a "constitution") and AI feedback (RLAIF) rather than relying on human labels for harmlessness; resulting models are more helpful and harmless than RLHF-only training and reduce the need for human red-teaming labels.
Methodology: Two phases: (1) supervised critique-revision phase in which the model critiques and revises its own outputs against the constitutional principles to build a dataset of AI-generated revisions; (2) RL phase in which a preference model is trained on AI-generated comparisons (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback, RLAIF) and used to fine-tune the policy via RL. Evaluation includes red-teaming for harmlessness.

--- Paper 4: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ---
Title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
Authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn (NeurIPS 2023; arXiv 2305.18290)
Contribution: Introduces DPO, which optimizes the same objective as RLHF without training a separate reward model or running an RL loop; alignment is recast as a simple classification problem over preference pairs. DPO matches or exceeds PPO-based RLHF on summarization (TL;DR) and dialogue while being simpler and more stable to train.
Methodology: Leverages a closed-form mapping between reward functions and optimal policies under a KL-constrained objective, so the optimal policy can be optimized directly. Training uses a binary cross-entropy objective over preferred/dispreferred completion pairs; no sampling from the LM during fine-tuning and no significant hyperparameter tuning. Experiments compare DPO against PPO-based RLHF on summarization and dialogue tasks.

--- Paper 5: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ---
Title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
Authors: John Schulman, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alec Radford, Oleg Klimov (arXiv 2017; arXiv 1707.06347)
Contribution: Foundational reinforcement learning algorithm paper: PPO is the policy-gradient RL method used as the RL stage in RLHF pipelines (InstructGPT, summarization). It simplifies trust region policy optimization (TRPO) while retaining its benefits, with better sample complexity; note the paper itself is about the RL algorithm, not language models.
Methodology: PPO alternates between sampling data via environment interaction and optimizing a clipped surrogate objective: L^CLIP = E[min(r_t * A_t, clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) * A_t)], where r_t is the probability ratio of new to old policy and A_t the advantage estimate; clipping prevents destructive large updates. Multiple epochs of minibatch updates per data sample; objective also includes a value-function loss and entropy bonus. Evaluated on Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks against other policy gradient methods.

Slide 8 (Summary): "Key Themes Across Papers" — synthesize: (1) human preferences as the signal: reward models trained on human comparisons are used to align LMs (InstructGPT, Summarization); (2) PPO as the standard RL optimizer for the RLHF stage; (3) reducing reliance on human labels: Constitutional AI uses AI feedback (RLAIF) and a constitution; (4) simplifying the pipeline: DPO shows alignment can be done without a separate reward model or RL loop; (5) the goal of alignment: more helpful, truthful, and harmless models that follow user intent.

Implementation notes:
- Use python-pptx: from pptx import Presentation; from pptx.util import Inches, Pt. Use the default template's layouts (layout 0 = title slide, layout 1 = title+content). For paper slides, put the paper title in the title placeholder and the rest (authors, venue/arXiv, contribution, methodology) as bullet paragraphs in the content placeholder. Set font sizes so text fits (title ~28-32pt, body ~12-16pt). Keep every bullet short enough to fit on one slide.
- Save exactly to `/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-conference-prep/workspace/RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx`.
- Print a confirmation of slide count and the save path from the script.

STEP 2 — Verify the saved deck with the pptx read tools (mcp__pptx__open_presentation on the saved path, then mcp__pptx__get_presentation_info and mcp__pptx__extract_presentation_text). Confirm: 8 slides; slide 1 title text; slide 2 overview; slides 3-7 cover all five frozen papers (check each paper title/authors appear); slide 8 synthesis. 

Return to the main agent: the absolute path of the saved file, the verified slide count, the list of slide titles as read back, and confirmation that all five papers' titles and author names appear on their slides (or report any discrepancies). Do not create calendar events or emails.
